excerpt: The Class 11 mid-term is the first paper that feels like the board pattern, and most students walk in unsure what is even on it. Here is exactly what CBSE tests in the half-yearly, how to prepare, and a free 8-question mock to check yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
The Class 11 mid-term catches a lot of students off guard. It is the first Maths paper written in the full board style — three hours, 80 marks, an actual marking scheme — and it lands about halfway through the year, when most students have only just found their footing after the jump from Class 10. Every October I hear the same thing from students in Delhi and smaller towns alike: ‘I understood the chapters, but the paper still surprised me.’ That surprise is almost always about pattern and pacing, not about knowing the maths.

So this post does two things. First, it lays out what a CBSE Class 11 Maths mid-term (Mock Test I) actually covers and how the marks are split. Then it gives you a free 8-question mock quiz, pitched at exactly this level, so you can test yourself before the real thing.

What the Class 11 mid-term usually covers

The half-yearly is built from the first-half chapters of the NCERT syllabus. Schools vary by a chapter or two, but a typical CBSE Class 11 Maths mid-term draws from:

  • Sets — subsets, power sets, Venn diagrams, union and intersection, the number of subsets rule (2n).
  • Relations and Functions — ordered pairs, Cartesian products, domain and range, and the common function types.
  • Trigonometric Functions — radian measure, signs in each quadrant, standard values, and identities like sin2θ + cos2θ = 1.
  • Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations — powers of i, modulus and conjugate, and roots with a negative discriminant.
  • Linear Inequalities — solving one-variable inequalities and showing the solution on a number line.
  • Permutations and Combinations — the counting principle, factorials, and when order matters versus when it does not.
  • Sequences and Series — arithmetic and geometric progressions, the nth term, and sums.

If your school has moved faster, Straight Lines or the Binomial Theorem may sneak in too. Check your own syllabus circular — but the seven chapters above are the reliable core.

The 80-mark scheme, section by section

CBSE follows one blueprint across the year, and the mid-term copies it. Knowing the shape of the paper is half the battle, because it tells you how long to spend where.

SectionQuestion typeMarks eachRoughly
AMCQs and assertion-reason120 marks
BVery short answer210 marks
CShort answer318 marks
DLong answer520 marks
ECase-study / source-based412 marks

Two things students miss. Section A is 20 marks of one-mark questions — that is a quarter of the paper decided by quick recall and small calculations, so a silly slip there hurts as much as a wrong five-marker. And the case-study section rewards reading carefully; the maths inside it is usually easier than a Section D question, but only if you extract the right numbers from the passage.

How to prepare (what actually moves the needle)

I am going to be blunt about what works, because most mid-term revision advice is just ‘study harder.’

Master the standard values first

Trigonometric values for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, the powers of i (i, −1, −i, 1, repeating), and the subset count 2n are cheap marks that appear every single year. Get these automatic and Section A stops being scary.

Practise NCERT exercises, then previous mid-terms

The NCERT solved examples and exercises are the backbone — CBSE questions are modelled on them. Once those feel routine, work through two or three past half-yearly papers under a timer. The NCERT Class 11 Mathematics textbook is the free, official source, and the exam design comes straight from CBSE.

Write, do not just read

Complex numbers and P&C in particular punish passive revision. You can follow a solved permutation problem perfectly and still freeze when the numbers change. Solve with a pen.

Budget your three hours before you start

A useful rule for the real paper: roughly a minute per mark, which leaves about twenty minutes at the end to revisit flagged questions and check the one-markers. If a Section D problem is not moving after four or five minutes, mark it and come back — leaving three easy Section A questions unread to chase one hard proof is the most common way students lose marks they had already earned. Attempt the questions you are sure of first, then circle back.

How to use a mock test properly

A mock is only useful if you treat it like the real paper, then mine it for mistakes afterwards. My routine:

  • Time it. Even a short quiz — give yourself a fixed window and do not pause.
  • Attempt everything before checking anything. Checking answer-by-answer flatters your score and teaches you nothing.
  • Sort your errors. A wrong answer is either a concept gap (you did not know the method) or a slip (you knew it but miscalculated). The two need different fixes — revise for the first, slow down for the second.
  • Redo the misses a day later from a blank page. If you can, the fix stuck.

One honest caveat: do not measure yourself on a single mock. Scores swing with the exact questions. It is the pattern across three or four attempts — which chapter keeps costing you marks — that tells you where to spend your last week.

quiz.title: Class 11 Maths Mid-Term Mock Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions across the mid-term core — sets, trigonometry, complex numbers, inequalities, permutations, combinations and progressions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: CBSE Class 11 Maths mid-term (half-yearly) core chapters

questions.q: A set A has 3 elements. How many subsets does it have?
questions.explanation: A set with n elements has 2 to the power n subsets. Here 2 cubed is 8 (this includes the empty set and A itself).

questions.q: What is the value of sin 30° + cos 60°?
questions.explanation: sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 60° = 1/2, so the sum is 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.

questions.q: What is the value of i to the power 4?
questions.explanation: Powers of i cycle every four: i, −1, −i, 1. Since i squared = −1, i to the fourth = (i squared) squared = (−1) squared = 1.
Subtract 1: 2x > 4. Divide by 2 (positive, so the sign stays): x > 2.

questions.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1 to 9 with no digit repeated?
questions.explanation: By the counting principle: 9 choices for the first digit, 8 for the second, 7 for the third. 9 × 8 × 7 = 504.

questions.q: What is the value of C(5, 2), the number of ways to choose 2 items from 5?
questions.explanation: C(5, 2) = 5! / (2! × 3!) = (5 × 4) / (2 × 1) = 10. Order does not matter, so it is a combination, not a permutation.

questions.q: In the arithmetic progression 2, 5, 8, 11, ..., what is the 10th term?
questions.explanation: First term a = 2, common difference d = 3. The nth term is a + (n − 1)d = 2 + 9 × 3 = 2 + 27 = 29.

questions.q: What is the modulus of the complex number 3 + 4i?
questions.explanation: The modulus of a + bi is the square root of (a squared + b squared) = square root of (9 + 16) = square root of 25 = 5.

faq.q: Which chapters come in the Class 11 Maths mid-term?
faq.a: Most CBSE schools test the first-half chapters: Sets, Relations and Functions, Trigonometric Functions, Complex Numbers, Linear Inequalities, Permutations and Combinations, and Sequences and Series. Straight Lines or the Binomial Theorem may be added if your school has moved faster — always confirm from your school’s syllabus circular.

faq.q: How many marks is the Class 11 mid-term out of?
faq.a: The written paper is 80 marks over 3 hours, following the CBSE board blueprint — Section A (1-mark MCQs), B (2 marks), C (3 marks), D (5 marks) and E (4-mark case studies). Internal assessment carries the remaining 20 marks.

faq.q: How should I prepare for the Class 11 Maths mid-term?
faq.a: Lock down the standard values first — trigonometric ratios, powers of i, the 2 to the power n subset rule — then work every NCERT exercise, and finish with two or three timed past papers. Writing solutions by hand beats re-reading them, especially for complex numbers and permutations.

faq.q: Is a mock test actually useful, or should I just revise more?
faq.a: A mock is useful only if you time it, attempt everything before checking, and then sort your errors into concept gaps versus careless slips. Those two need different fixes. Judge yourself on the pattern across several mocks, not a single score, which swings with the exact questions.
